intro: Sirens on a spring night. A field so flat you can see the next town's water tower. A shadow that shrinks and swings across the blacktop. A river that flows the wrong way. Every one of those is a clue. This unit is about Earth: its weather, its ground, its place in space, and the people living on it.

You will measure weather with real tools. You will find the pattern hiding in a year of numbers. You will read a cliff like a book, oldest page on the bottom. You will find out why Illinois is flat and why the sun seems to move. You will learn why summer is not about being closer to the sun. And you will see where all of Earth's water really is.

By the end, you can explain a tornado warning and a pothole. You can explain a shadow stick, a full moon and a backward river. And you can argue with evidence about a hard question. When people change Earth's systems, what happens next? Who has to live with it?
bigQuestion: What patterns shape Earth's weather, land and sky, and how do people fit into those systems?

timeline.t: Copernicus publishes the idea that Earth circles the sun, not the other way around.
Galileo turns a telescope on the moon and sees mountains and craters.
Benjamin Franklin works out that a storm traveled up the coast as a whole.
James Hutton argues that slow, everyday processes shaped the land over vast time.
Luke Howard names the clouds: cumulus, stratus and cirrus.
John Wesley Powell rides the Colorado River through the Grand Canyon, reading its layers.
The United States starts a national weather service to warn of storms.
Chicago opens its canal and the Chicago River flows away from Lake Michigan.
The Tri-State Tornado crosses Missouri, Illinois and Indiana, the deadliest in U.S. history.
Apollo 11 lands on the moon; astronauts hop in its weaker gravity.
The first Earth Day; new laws soon limit pollution of rivers and air.
Mount St. Helens erupts, changing a mountain in minutes.

words.d: what the air is doing at one place and time: temperature, wind, clouds and rain
the usual weather of a place, found by averaging many years of measurements
water that falls from clouds as rain, snow, sleet or hail
a prediction of the weather to come, based on measurements and computer models
the breaking of rock into smaller pieces by ice, water, plants or heat
the carrying away of rock pieces and soil by water, wind, ice or gravity
the dropping of rock pieces and soil when water, wind or ice slows down
a huge mass of ice that moves slowly over land
Earth spinning around its axis once every 24 hours, making day and night
the path one object takes around another, like Earth around the sun each year
the pull that draws everything toward the center of Earth or another large object
all of Earth's water: oceans, lakes, rivers, ice and water underground

test.q: Which statement is about climate rather than weather?
test.why: Climate is the usual pattern over many years; the others describe one day.

choices: conditions are right for a tornado
a tornado will hit next week
a tornado has been spotted or seen on radar; take shelter now
test.why: A warning means it is happening. A watch means be ready.
An anemometer's spinning cups measure how fast the wind blows.

test.q: In an undisturbed stack of rock layers, the oldest layer is
test.why: New layers form on top of old ones, so the bottom is the oldest.

test.q: Freezing water widens a crack in a rock. This is
test.why: Weathering breaks rock in place. Ice wedging is one kind.

test.q: A river slows down at a lake and drops its mud. This is
test.why: Deposition is the dropping of carried material when moving water slows.

test.q: Why is most of Illinois flat?
choices: Glaciers buried the old hills under thick till
test.why: Melting ice sheets dropped a deep blanket of till over the older land.

test.q: On a world map, earthquakes and volcanoes mostly
choices: line up in belts where plates meet
test.why: They cluster along plate boundaries, such as the Ring of Fire.
Earth spins once a day, turning each place into sunlight and out again.

test.q: Why is it summer in Illinois in July?
choices: Earth is closest to the sun in July
Illinois is tilted toward the sun, so sunlight hits more directly
The sun is hotter in July
The moon is full more often
test.why: The tilt of Earth's axis, not distance, makes summer sunlight direct and days long.

test.q: A shadow stick's shadow is shortest
test.why: When the sun is highest, near noon, the shadow is shortest.

test.q: Why does the sun look so much brighter than other stars?
choices: It is the only star that makes light
It is much closer to Earth
It is made of different gas
test.why: The sun is an ordinary star that is millions of times closer than any other.

test.q: About what share of Earth's water is fresh?
test.why: Roughly 97 percent is salty ocean; only about 3 percent is fresh.

test.q: Which sphere are you changing when you plant a tree in an empty lot?
choices: The biosphere, and through it the others
test.why: Adding a living thing changes the biosphere, and its roots, leaves and shade affect soil, water and air.

test.q: What was the main trade-off of reversing the Chicago River in 1900?
choices: Boats could no longer use it
Cleaner drinking water for Chicago, but waste sent to towns downstream
test.why: Chicago's water got safer while the Illinois River towns received the city's waste.

write.prompt: Chicago reversed its river in 1900 to protect its drinking water. Make a claim: was it the right decision? Support it with evidence from the unit about Earth's systems and how they connect, and explain your reasoning.
tips: Claim: state clearly whether the reversal was the right choice, or right but not enough.
Evidence: use facts from the story and lessons, such as disease in Chicago before 1900, where the waste went after, and later fixes like treatment plants.
Reasoning: connect the evidence to the four spheres. Show how a change in the hydrosphere reached the biosphere.
The other side: say what someone in a downstream town might argue, and answer it.
Use the words trade-off, downstream and system at least once each.
